title: NASA’s New 3D Model Shows the Earth Is a Lumpy Mess
gist: NASA published a geoid visualization exaggerating Earth's gravitational variations 10,000-fold, built from 15 years and a billion satellite observations. The underlying GRACE gravimetry program yields hard numbers — Antarctica losing ~135 gigatons of ice a year and Greenland 264 gigatons from 2002 to 2025 — and is now detecting the record-low soil moisture behind this summer's fires in Spain and France.

themes.theme: The geoid model and how it was built

insights.claim: NASA has released a geoid model showing the shape of Earth's gravitational field, where irregular bulges and depressions reflect uneven distribution of mass inside the planet and can be read as the surface a global ocean would take under gravity and rotation alone.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: A mental model for reading gravity data as a proxy for subsurface mass — the same logic underpinning water and ice monitoring.
insights.locator: NASA has released a new geoid model

insights.claim: The visualization exaggerates geoid heights by a factor of 10,000 to make gravitational variation visible, meaning the dramatic lumpiness is a display artifact rather than physical shape.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Guard against over-reading the visual: the underlying signal is subtle and requires satellite-grade precision to detect.
insights.locator: The visualization is an exaggerated geoid

insights.claim: The model draws on 15 years of satellite data comprising roughly a billion observations, produced with science advisor Scott Luthcke and visualizer Mark SubbaRao of NASA Goddard.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Long-baseline, high-volume geodetic datasets are a public-good asset that private climate-risk analytics depend on.

insights.claim: GRACE satellite observations show Antarctica losing approximately 135 gigatons of ice per year and Greenland losing 264 gigatons annually between 2002 and 2025.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Hard, decades-long mass-loss numbers are the empirical base for sea-level rise projections that drive coastal insurance and infrastructure pricing.
insights.locator: NASA’s satellites—which operate as part of the Gravity Recovery

insights.claim: Improving ice-loss estimates is framed as key to understanding how much oceans are rising now and how much more they will rise in the future.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Measurement precision directly propagates into sea-level forecast uncertainty — the input variable behind long-dated climate risk models.

insights.claim: Both NASA and the European Space Agency operate satellites that monitor Earth's gravitational field, so the capability is not single-agency dependent.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Redundant transatlantic monitoring capacity reduces the risk that a single budget decision blinds climate measurement.
insights.locator: NASA and the European Space Agency both have satellites

themes.theme: Gravity data as a water and drought instrument

insights.claim: GRACE observations are used to track groundwater loss and drought globally, and the data shows long-term groundwater depletion in the western US and elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Satellite gravimetry is an independent, hard-to-manipulate measure of aquifer depletion — relevant to water rights, agriculture and utility siting in the US West.
insights.locator: The GRACE observations have also been used to track groundwater loss

insights.claim: The extreme dryness fueling this summer's fires in Spain and France is visible in GRACE's data, showing the system captures acute droughts and not only long-term trends.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Near-real-time drought detection from orbit is a live input for European agricultural and wildfire risk pricing.
insights.locator: It also provides information on more acute droughts

insights.claim: A University of Nebraska analysis using gravitational observations finds soil moisture and shallow groundwater sitting in or near record-low territory in parts of the affected region.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Record-low soil moisture is a leading indicator for European crop yields and for repeat wildfire seasons.
insights.locator: An analysis from the University of Nebraska

insights.claim: With climate change set to make drought worse in many locations, these gravitational observations are positioned as valuable operational information for water managers in parched regions.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Institutional demand for satellite-derived water data should grow structurally — a tailwind for earth-observation data services.
insights.locator: With climate change set to make drought worse
